definition: Pipelines are categorized by distance/role: transportation pipelines move gas long distances with relatively simple (one or two branch) structures, while distribution pipelines deliver gas to end-users through complex branching networks and are more expensive to build/operate per unit distance, especially over 'the last mile' from a citygate to a consumer.
core_idea: The complexity (and thus cost) of a pipeline is driven more by how many end-users it must reach than by the distance it spans, so short last-mile distribution segments can cost as much as moving gas across the entire country.
key_points: Transportation pipelines: long-distance, structurally simple (few branches).
Distribution pipelines: deliver to many end-users, structurally complex due to branching.
Last-mile delivery cost (citygate to consumer) can rival the cost of long-distance cross-country transport.
relationships: Connects to hub/citygate definitions and to burner-tip pricing.
trading_implications: Local distribution costs are a material component of delivered gas price, not just long-haul transport - relevant when evaluating citygate vs. burner-tip pricing.
caveats: That cost scales mainly with distance - the source emphasizes branching complexity, not distance, drives distribution cost.
